CODICIL TO A WILL
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Alameda County

DECLARATION IDENTIFYING THE ORIGINAL WILL AND THE AMENDMENT
I, Jordan Alex Lee, of Alameda County, declare this instrument to be a codicil to my Last Will and Testament dated January 15, 2024 (the "Will"). I identify below the specific provision(s) of the Will that this codicil adds, deletes, or amends: ☐ _________________________. Except as specifically changed by this codicil, I confirm and republish the Will, and all of its provisions not specifically amended by this codicil, in all other respects.

WHAT A CODICIL IS UNDER CALIFORNIA LAW
California's Probate Code treats a codicil not as a separate category of legal instrument with its own rules, but as a type of will. The Probate Code's general definitions provide that the term "will" includes a codicil, and that these definitions govern the construction of the Probate Code's provisions unless context requires otherwise. As a result, any Probate Code statute that refers to a "will" — including execution formalities, revocation rules, and revival rules — presumptively applies to a codicil, such as this one executed by Jordan Alex Lee of Alameda County, in the same way it applies to the original will.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "“Will” includes codicil and any testamentary instrument which merely appoints an executor or revokes or revises another will."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 88 (California Legislative Information text), definition of 'will' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=88)
  "Unless the provision or context otherwise requires, the definitions in this part govern the construction of this code."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 20 (California Legislative Information text), definitions govern construction of the code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=20)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how "codicil" is defined and treated in relation to "will" — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific codicil. The definition itself (Probate Code § 88) is a single sentence with no further codicil-specific elaboration; this clause does not overstate its brevity into something more detailed than the statute provides.

A CODICIL MUST INDEPENDENTLY SATISFY WILL-EXECUTION FORMALITIES
Because "will" is statutorily defined to include "codicil," a codicil to Jordan Alex Lee's will dated January 15, 2024 is not exempt from the formalities that apply to wills generally. Probate Code § 6110 requires that a will be in writing and satisfy the section's signature and witnessing requirements. A codicil that fails to independently meet these formalities does not receive any special exemption from them merely because it amends, rather than replaces, an already-valid will.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Except as provided in this part, a will shall be in writing and satisfy the requirements of this section."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 6110(a) (California Legislative Information text), execution of wills (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6110)
  "“Will” includes codicil and any testamentary instrument which merely appoints an executor or revokes or revises another will."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 88 (California Legislative Information text), definition of 'will' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=88)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the execution requirements applicable to a codicil — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific codicil. The full detail of California's signature and witnessing requirements (including the two-witness rule and the harmless-error exception) is addressed at length in this project's companion Last Will and Testament document and is not re-derived here; this clause states only that a codicil is not exempt from those requirements, not what all of their details are.

REVOKING A CODICIL DOES NOT AUTOMATICALLY REVIVE WHAT IT CHANGED
If a codicil that revoked or changed part of Jordan Alex Lee's will dated January 15, 2024 is itself later revoked, the terms of the original will that the codicil had changed are not automatically restored. California's revival statute provides that when a later testamentary instrument that would have revoked part of an earlier one is itself thereafter revoked, the earlier instrument's revoked terms are revived only if it is evident from the circumstances of the later instrument's revocation, or from the testator's contemporaneous or subsequent declarations, that the testator intended the earlier terms to take effect as originally executed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "If a second will which, had it remained effective at death, would have revoked the first will in whole or in part, is thereafter revoked by acts under Section 6120 or 6121, the first will is revoked in whole or in part unless it is evident from the circumstances of the revocation of the second will or from the testator’s contemporary or subsequent declarations that the testator intended the first will to take effect as executed."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 6123(a) (California Legislative Information text), revival (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6123)
  "A will or any part thereof is revoked by any of the following: (a) A subsequent will which revokes the prior will or part expressly or by inconsistency."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 6120(a) (California Legislative Information text), revocation by subsequent will (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6120)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's revival rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific codicil. Probate Code § 6120, which defines revocation generally, does not itself use the word "codicil" and does not separately address the scenario of two physically distinct paper instruments (an original will and a separate codicil document) — it is Probate Code § 88's definitional inclusion of "codicil" within "will" that extends §§ 6120 and 6123 to codicils at all. Neither § 6120 nor § 6123 expressly states, in so many words, whether physically revoking the original will instrument automatically revokes a separate codicil to it, or the reverse; that specific multi-document question is not resolved by the statutory text found.

A LATER CODICIL INCONSISTENT WITH AN EARLIER INSTRUMENT
California's Probate Code does not contain a statute written specifically for the scenario of a later codicil that conflicts with an earlier codicil or with the original will. Two general principles govern instead. First, a subsequent testamentary instrument revokes a prior one, in whole or in part, "expressly or by inconsistency" — a rule that, because "will" includes "codicil," applies to a later codicil in relation to an earlier one or to the original will. Second, general rules of construction direct that all parts of an instrument be construed in relation to each other so as, if possible, to form a consistent whole, with any ambiguity resolved by reference to other parts of the instrument.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A will or any part thereof is revoked by any of the following: (a) A subsequent will which revokes the prior will or part expressly or by inconsistency."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 6120(a) (California Legislative Information text), revocation by inconsistency (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6120)
  "All parts of an instrument are to be construed in relation to each other and so as, if possible, to form a consistent whole. If the meaning of any part of an instrument is ambiguous or doubtful, it may be explained by any reference to or recital of that part in another part of the instrument."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21121 (California Legislative Information text), construing an instrument as a consistent whole (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21121)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California addresses conflicting testamentary provisions — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific codicil. Beyond the general "expressly or by inconsistency" revocation rule and the general construction principles cited here, no codicil-specific inconsistency statute was found in the Probate Code's Division 6 or Division 11.

A LOST CODICIL IS PRESUMED REVOKED, SEPARATELY FROM THE WILL
California law presumes that a will last in the testator's possession, which cannot be found after the testator's death, was destroyed by the testator with intent to revoke it. Because "will" includes "codicil," this presumption applies separately to a codicil that was last in Jordan Alex Lee's possession and cannot be located after death, independent of whether the original will dated January 15, 2024 is itself found.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "If the testator’s will was last in the testator’s possession, the testator was competent until death, and neither the will nor a duplicate original of the will can be found after the testator’s death, it is presumed that the testator destroyed the will with intent to revoke it. This presumption is a presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 6124 (California Legislative Information text), presumption of revocation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6124)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's lost-instrument presumption — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific codicil. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 6124); no additional independent source was found for this.

SIGNATURE AND WITNESS BLOCK
Signed by Jordan Alex Lee as a codicil to the Will dated January 15, 2024, on September 1, 2026, at Alameda County, California.

We, the undersigned, being at least two in number, each declare under penalty of perjury that Jordan Alex Lee, in our presence and in the presence of each other, signed this codicil, or acknowledged the signature or the codicil already made, and declared to us that it is Jordan Alex Lee's codicil; that we understood this instrument to be Jordan Alex Lee's codicil; and that we, and each of us, in Jordan Alex Lee's presence and at Jordan Alex Lee's request, and in the presence of each other, sign our names below as witnesses.

Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________
Witness 1 — Signature: ☐ _________________________ Printed name: ☐ _________________________
Witness 2 — Signature: ☐ _________________________ Printed name: ☐ _________________________
